Fuel for Petrol Engines
Petrol is a common liquid fuel used for two and four-wheeler light passenger vehicles. It is a mixture of about 150 volatile hydrocarbons with carbon atoms between 4 to 12 per molecule. Petrol contains straight and branched-chain alkanes (paraffins), cyclic alkanes (naphthenes), unsaturated hydrocarbons with one double bond (olefins) and aromatic hydrocarbons, with an average chemical composition of C8.26H15.5.
This problem will explore combustion of petrol and related fuels being used commercially in petrol engines. Some useful data:

| Compound | Density (g cm–3) | ΔH°combustion (kJ mol–1) |
|---|---|---|
| n-octane (l) | 0.70 | ‒ 5470.3 |
| cyclohexane (l) | 0.77 | ‒ 3918.6 |
| isooctane (l) | 0.69 | ‒ 5461.0 |
| ethanol (l) | 0.79 | ‒ 1366.8 |

PART A: Combustion in Petrol Engines
The combustion of petrol can be understood with octane as a model fuel.
1.1 Draw structures of all possible stereoisomer(s) of octane having two chiral centers, in the wedge-dash representation.

The combustion of fuel starts with a homolytic cleavage of a C–H bond in a hydrocarbon, forming alkyl radicals. These radicals can undergo rearrangement to form more stable radicals. If the radicals generated are unstable even after rearrangement, the fuel can burn at low temperatures. Among the alkyl radicals generated by the octane isomers during combustion, those formed by isooctane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) are most stable, some of which are stabilized by rearrangement.
1.2. Draw the structure(s) of all probable alkyl radical(s) that are formed from isooctane including those after rearrangement. Identify the most stable free radical by circling its structure.

In a petrol engine under certain conditions, some components of the fuel-air mixture forming less-stable free radicals may self-ignite without ignition by the primary flame front as shown in the diagram below. Such secondary flames outside the primary flame front create secondary heat and pressure waves. Multiple pressure waves in the cylinder can create shock waves and cause jerky movements of the piston. The shock waves also create a characteristic "pinging" sound, known as knocking. Knocking tendency of a fuel (causing jerky movements in vehicle) is quantified by octane number. The fuel that causes less knocking is considered better and is assigned a higher octane number.

[Diagram description: Two side-by-side diagrams of a petrol engine cylinder. The left diagram, labeled "Smooth combustion", shows a spark plug igniting the fuel mixture, creating a single, smooth "Primary Flame" front that expands downwards towards the piston. The right diagram, labeled "Knocking", shows a similar cylinder where the spark plug ignites a "Primary Flame", but a "Secondary flame front" has spontaneously ignited at the side of the cylinder, separate from the primary flame, creating multiple flame fronts.]

1.3. Arrange the following hydrocarbons in ascending order of their knocking tendency.
methylcyclohexane, isooctane, n-octane, toluene (methylbenzene)

1.4. Estimate the stoichiometric amount of air (in g) required for the complete combustion of 100 cm3 of a liquid fuel mixture containing n-octane and cyclohexane [70:30, v/v assuming volumes are additive]. Write balanced equations for the combustion of each component. Assume composition of air (v/v) at NTP as: Argon (0.95%), Nitrogen (78.08%) & Oxygen (20.95%).

Air-fuel ratio (λ) is the relative stoichiometric ratio between the mass of air and the mass of fuel that are injected in the engine. When λ = 1, the combustion mixture in the engine contains a stoichiometric amount of air and fuel; values of λ < 1 signify fuel-rich mixtures, while λ > 1 correspond to air-rich mixtures. This ratio affects the composition of emitted gases from the engine.

Concentration values of two gases in a petrol engine exhaust as a function of λ are presented as two curves in the graph here.
[Graph description: A line graph showing "Exhaust gas emissions (ppm)" on the y-axis versus "λ" on the x-axis. The x-axis ranges from 0.70 to 1.20. The y-axis ranges from 0.0 to 400.0. There are two unlabeled curves. Curve 1 starts at approximately 250 ppm at λ = 0.72, and steadily decreases as λ increases, reaching approximately 120 ppm at λ = 1.18. Curve 2 starts at approximately 40 ppm at λ = 0.72, increases to a peak of approximately 360 ppm around λ = 1.10, and then decreases to approximately 290 ppm at λ = 1.18.]

1.5. If 20% excess air (λ = 1.2) is injected in a petrol engine for combustion of a fuel mixture containing octane (85% v/v), cyclohexane (5% v/v), 2-butene (5% v/v) and toluene (5% v/v), identify the gases emitted in the exhaust in significant concentrations (above 200 ppm). Mark X for the correct option(s).
a) CO2
b) CO
c) Ar
d) NOx
e) N2
f) O2
g) unburnt hydrocarbons (HC)

PART B: Mixing Ethanol with Isooctane
Most governments have been imposing vehicle emissions regulations that are continually being tightened further. BS VI emission standards notified by the Government of India limit values of exhaust gases for two wheelers fitted with spark ignition engines as follows: CO (500 mg km–1), HC (100 mg km–1), NOx (90 mg km–1).
[Reference: The Emission Standards for Bharat Stage VI (BS-VI), Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, May 2020].

Changing fuel compositions can address some of the emission concerns. Ethanol is one of the alternative transportation fuels which is available as a byproduct from agricultural sources.

1.6. Consider the liquid fuel for an engine is changed from isooctane (F0) to a mixture containing 80% isooctane and 20% ethanol (v/v, assuming volumes are additive), known as F20.
(i) Estimate the difference in calorific values of these two fuels, C (F20) – C (F0), heat released per g.
(ii) By what percent CO2 emission is reduced on changing the fuel from F0 to F20 for the same distance covered by the vehicle? Assume 100% efficient combustion and the efficiency of engines in the two cases to be identical.

PART C: Ethanol Blended Petrol
Ethanol blended petrol in different proportions is being used in different parts of the world including India. E85 is blend of 85% ethanol and 15% petrol, E20 is 20% ethanol blended with 80% petrol and so on. The ignition temperature of fuel is the temperature at which it spontaneously ignites in atmospheric air without an external source of ignition. Certain facts associated with ethanol blended fuels are:
F1. Ethanol forms an azeotrope with water.
F2. Addition of double bonds to alkyl chain of a fuel mixture stabilizes some of its alkyl radicals.
F3. Ethanol molecules are inherently rich in oxygen.
F4. The ignition temperature of ethanol is 365 °C and that of petrol is 247 - 280 °C.
F5. Ethanol-blended petrol absorbs water from atmosphere.
F6. Oxygen containing fuels inhibit formation of soot.
F7. Latent heat of evaporation of ethanol is much higher than that of octanes.

1.7. State which of the following statements are correct/ incorrect for petrol engines and write the fact/s (F1 - F7) which justify your answer.
S1. The E20 blended fuel will exhibit lower knocking than E0.
S2. Temperature of air fuel mixture in an engine at the start of combustion would be lower for E85 than for E20.
S3. E85 fuel can be more damaging to the engine parts having metallic surfaces than E20.
S4. E85 fuel will result in more emissions of unburnt HC than E20 fuel, at λ = 1.
S5. Emission of particulate matter is significantly increased with E85.

Below I give the requested reasoning and the final answers part by part.

---

## 1.1 Octane stereoisomers having **two chiral centers**

We need isomers of **C8H18** that contain **exactly two stereogenic carbons**, and then draw **all stereoisomers** of those structures.

Among octane isomers, the one that clearly has two chiral centers is:

- **3,4-dimethylhexane**

Structure:
CH3–CH2–CH(CH3)–CH(CH3)–CH2–CH3

Here C-3 and C-4 are both chiral.

Because the molecule is symmetric, its stereoisomers are:

- **(3R,4R)**
- **(3S,4S)**
- **meso-(3R,4S) = (3S,4R)**

So there are **3 stereoisomers total**.

### Wedge-dash representation
Textually:

1. **(3R,4R)-3,4-dimethylhexane**  
   both methyl groups on wedges (or both on dashes, depending on drawing convention consistently)

2. **(3S,4S)-3,4-dimethylhexane**  
   mirror image of above

3. **meso-(3R,4S)-3,4-dimethylhexane**  
   one methyl on wedge and the other on dash

---

## 1.2 Alkyl radicals from isooctane and rearranged radicals

Isooctane = **2,2,4-trimethylpentane**

Structure:
CH3–C(CH3)2–CH2–CH(CH3)–CH3

Distinct H-abstraction positions give radicals at chemically different carbons.

### Primary radicals formed directly by H abstraction

1. **At C1/C equivalent methyl attached to quaternary C2**  
   Neopentyl-type primary radical:
   **·CH2–C(CH3)2–CH2–CH(CH3)–CH3**

   Also equivalent radicals from the two methyl substituents on C2:
   **CH3–C(CH2·)(CH3)–CH2–CH(CH3)–CH3**
   and equivalent one from the other methyl.

2. **At C3**
   Secondary radical:
   **CH3–C(CH3)2–CH·–CH(CH3)–CH3**

3. **At C4**
   Tertiary radical:
   **CH3–C(CH3)2–CH2–C·(CH3)–CH3**

4. **At terminal methyls attached to C4/C5**
   Primary radical:
   **CH3–C(CH3)2–CH2–CH(CH3)–CH2·**

and similarly from the methyl substituent on C4:
   **CH3–C(CH3)2–CH2–CH(CH2·)–CH3**

### Rearrangement
The less stable primary radicals can rearrange by H-shift / alkyl shift to more stable radicals, especially toward the **tertiary radical at C4**.

Thus the important radicals to include are:

- primary radicals (various)
- secondary radical at C3
- **tertiary radical at C4** after direct formation or rearrangement

### Most stable radical
Stability order is generally:
**tertiary > secondary > primary**

So the **most stable free radical** is:

**CH3–C(CH3)2–CH2–C·(CH3)–CH3**

This is the one to circle.

---

## 1.3 Ascending order of knocking tendency

Knocking tendency decreases as fuel forms more stable radicals / has higher octane number.

Known trends:
- **n-octane** knocks strongly
- **isooctane** has very low knocking tendency
- aromatics like **toluene** have very high octane number, very low knocking
- cycloalkanes are intermediate; methylcyclohexane better than n-octane but worse than isooctane/toluene

So ascending order of **knocking tendency** (least → most) is:

**toluene < isooctane < methylcyclohexane < n-octane**

---

## 1.4 Stoichiometric air for 100 cm³ fuel mixture

Fuel mixture:
- 70 cm³ n-octane
- 30 cm³ cyclohexane

Densities:
- n-octane = 0.70 g cm⁻³
- cyclohexane = 0.77 g cm⁻³

### Step 1: masses

#### n-octane
mass = 70 × 0.70 = **49.0 g**

Molar mass octane = 114 g mol⁻¹  
moles = 49.0 / 114 = **0.4298 mol**

#### cyclohexane
mass = 30 × 0.77 = **23.1 g**

Molar mass cyclohexane = 84 g mol⁻¹  
moles = 23.1 / 84 = **0.275 mol**

---

### Step 2: combustion equations

#### n-octane
\[
2C_8H_{18} + 25O_2 \rightarrow 16CO_2 + 18H_2O
\]

So 1 mol octane needs **12.5 mol O2**

#### cyclohexane
\[
C_6H_{12} + 9O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O
\]

So 1 mol cyclohexane needs **9 mol O2**

---

### Step 3: O2 needed

For octane:
\[
0.4298 \times 12.5 = 5.3725 \text{ mol O}_2
\]

For cyclohexane:
\[
0.275 \times 9 = 2.475 \text{ mol O}_2
\]

Total:
\[
5.3725 + 2.475 = 7.8475 \text{ mol O}_2
\]

Mass O2:
\[
7.8475 \times 32 = 251.12 \text{ g}
\]

---

### Step 4: convert O2 to air mass

Air contains 20.95% O2 by volume, hence by mole fraction approximately 0.2095.

Moles of air needed:
\[
n_{\text{air}} = \frac{7.8475}{0.2095} = 37.46 \text{ mol}
\]

Average molar mass of air:

\[
M = (0.2095)(32) + (0.7808)(28) + (0.0095)(40)
\]

\[
= 6.704 + 21.8624 + 0.38 = 28.9464 \text{ g mol}^{-1}
\]

Mass of air:
\[
37.46 \times 28.9464 \approx 1084 \text{ g}
\]

### Final answer
Stoichiometric air required for **100 cm³** of the fuel mixture:

\[
\boxed{1.08 \times 10^3 \text{ g air (approximately)}}
\]

---

## 1.5 Significant exhaust gases at λ = 1.2

At **20% excess air**, mixture is **lean**.

From the graph:
- one gas decreases with λ and is below 200 ppm at λ = 1.2 → this is **CO**
- another peaks near λ > 1 and is above 200 ppm at λ = 1.2 → this is **NOx**

Also, major exhaust components will certainly include:
- **CO2**
- **N2**
- **Ar**
- excess **O2**

Unburnt HC at λ = 1.2 is not indicated above 200 ppm from the graph.

So gases present in significant concentrations (>200 ppm) are:

- **CO2**
- **Ar**
- **NOx**
- **N2**
- **O2**

### Correct options
\[
\boxed{a,\ c,\ d,\ e,\ f}
\]

---

# PART B

## 1.6(i) Difference in calorific values, \( C(F20)-C(F0) \)

F0 = pure isooctane  
F20 = 80% isooctane + 20% ethanol by volume

Take **100 cm³** of each fuel.

---

### F0

100 cm³ isooctane

Mass:
\[
100 \times 0.69 = 69 \text{ g}
\]

Moles:
\[
69/114 = 0.6053 \text{ mol}
\]

Heat released:
\[
0.6053 \times 5461.0 = 3305 \text{ kJ}
\]

Calorific value:
\[
C(F0)=3305/69 = 47.9 \text{ kJ g}^{-1}
\]

---

### F20

#### Isooctane part: 80 cm³
Mass:
\[
80 \times 0.69 = 55.2 \text{ g}
\]

Moles:
\[
55.2/114 = 0.4842 \text{ mol}
\]

Heat:
\[
0.4842 \times 5461.0 = 2644 \text{ kJ}
\]

#### Ethanol part: 20 cm³
Mass:
\[
20 \times 0.79 = 15.8 \text{ g}
\]

Moles:
\[
15.8/46 = 0.3435 \text{ mol}
\]

Heat:
\[
0.3435 \times 1366.8 = 469.5 \text{ kJ}
\]

#### Total for F20
Mass:
\[
55.2 + 15.8 = 71.0 \text{ g}
\]

Heat:
\[
2644 + 469.5 = 3113.5 \text{ kJ}
\]

Calorific value:
\[
C(F20)=3113.5/71.0 = 43.9 \text{ kJ g}^{-1}
\]

### Difference
\[
C(F20)-C(F0)=43.9-47.9=-4.0 \text{ kJ g}^{-1}
\]

### Final answer
\[
\boxed{C(F20)-C(F0)\approx -4.0\ \text{kJ g}^{-1}}
\]

So F20 has a lower calorific value by about **4 kJ g⁻¹**.

---

## 1.6(ii) Percent reduction in CO2 emission for same distance

For same distance, assuming same engine efficiency, vehicle needs same total energy output.

So compare **CO2 emitted per unit heat released**.

---

### F0: isooctane only

Combustion:
\[
C_8H_{18} + \frac{25}{2}O_2 \to 8CO_2 + 9H_2O
\]

1 mol isooctane gives 8 mol CO2 and releases 5461 kJ.

CO2 per kJ:
\[
\frac{8}{5461} = 0.001465 \text{ mol kJ}^{-1}
\]

---

### F20

Using the 100 cm³ basis above:

- total heat = 3113.5 kJ

CO2 produced:

#### from isooctane
\[
0.4842 \times 8 = 3.8736 \text{ mol}
\]

#### from ethanol
\[
C_2H_5OH + 3O_2 \to 2CO_2 + 3H_2O
\]
\[
0.3435 \times 2 = 0.6870 \text{ mol}
\]

Total CO2:
\[
3.8736 + 0.6870 = 4.5606 \text{ mol}
\]

CO2 per kJ:
\[
\frac{4.5606}{3113.5} = 0.001465 \text{ mol kJ}^{-1}
\]

This is essentially the same.

Therefore for same distance and same efficiency, **CO2 emission is practically unchanged**.

### Final answer
\[
\boxed{0\% \text{ reduction (approximately)}}
\]

---

# PART C

## 1.7 Correct/incorrect statements with supporting facts

We use F1–F7.

---

### S1. “The E20 blended fuel will exhibit lower knocking than E0.”

E20 contains ethanol. Ethanol has higher ignition temperature than petrol and oxygenated fuels generally improve anti-knock behavior. Also lower petrol fraction reduces easy self-ignition.

So **Correct**.

Justified by:
- **F4**: ethanol ignition temperature (365 °C) is much higher than petrol (247–280 °C)

\[
\boxed{\text{S1 Correct — F4}}
\]

---

### S2. “Temperature of air fuel mixture in an engine at the start of combustion would be lower for E85 than for E20.”

More ethanol means stronger cooling on evaporation because ethanol has much larger latent heat of vaporization.

So **Correct**.

Justified by:
- **F7**: latent heat of evaporation of ethanol is much higher than that of octanes

\[
\boxed{\text{S2 Correct — F7}}
\]

---

### S3. “E85 fuel can be more damaging to the engine parts having metallic surfaces than E20.”

Higher ethanol blend absorbs more water; water + ethanol can promote corrosion of metallic parts.

So **Correct**.

Justified by:
- **F5**: ethanol-blended petrol absorbs water from atmosphere
- **F1**: ethanol forms azeotrope with water

\[
\boxed{\text{S3 Correct — F1, F5}}
\]

---

### S4. “E85 fuel will result in more emissions of unburnt HC than E20 fuel, at λ = 1.”

Ethanol has higher ignition temperature, so more difficult to ignite completely; also stronger charge cooling lowers initial mixture temperature. Hence higher ethanol blend can leave more unburnt HC.

So **Correct**.

Justified by:
- **F4**: ethanol has higher ignition temperature
- **F7**: ethanol has higher latent heat of evaporation, lowering mixture temperature

\[
\boxed{\text{S4 Correct — F4, F7}}
\]

---

### S5. “Emission of particulate matter is significantly increased with E85.”

Oxygen-containing fuels inhibit soot formation, so particulate matter should decrease, not increase.

So **Incorrect**.

Justified by:
- **F3**: ethanol molecules are inherently rich in oxygen
- **F6**: oxygen-containing fuels inhibit formation of soot

\[
\boxed{\text{S5 Incorrect — F3, F6}}
\]

Urinary Amylase

Amylase is an enzyme that hydrolyses starch into smaller carbohydrates such as glucose, maltose, maltotriose (containing 3 glucose units), and oligosaccharides (containing a few units of glucose). Over time, amylase may also break oligosaccharides, maltotriose, etc into glucose units. It is present in plant and animal bodies supporting starch metabolism. Very small concentrations of amylase or other enzymes may be found in human and animal urines.

[Figure: Structure of Starch. A polymer of glucose units. The image shows a glucose unit in a pyranose ring, linked via an alpha-1,4-glycosidic bond to the next unit, enclosed in brackets with subscript 'n'.]

However, if the pancreas is diseased or injured, amylase may get into blood and later in urine. Thus, an increased level of amylase in urine is an indicator of pancreatic dysfunction.

In a biochemical training course, students were trying different analytical methods for urine analysis. Urine samples were obtained from two persons, one of whom was having pancreatic dysfunction. These urine samples were diluted 10 times and the diluted samples U1 and U2 were given to three students, who used different approaches to analyze the samples.

Student 1 : To 10 mL each of U1 and U2 in two test tubes, he added 2 mL of 1% starch solution. After keeping these mixtures for 10 minutes, he added 2 mL of Tollen’s reagent and placed the test tubes in a hot water bath. In 30 minutes, both test tubes developed a silver mirror.

iii. She ran the chromatogram using butanol-water mixture as eluent, with small amount of acetic acid added (to enhance miscibility of butanol in water).
iv. She dried the plate and then dipped it in 0.1% AgNO3 solution, followed by a dip in 2 M NaOH solution. The plate turned completely brownish black.

(C) increased mobility of compounds with increased number of -OH groups per unit molar mass.

Student 3 : She followed Steps i-iii as student 2 but after running the TLC, dipped the TLC plate in a mixture of conc. sulphuric acid with phenol. ## 4.1 Structure of maltose
Maltose is **α-D-glucopyranosyl-(1→4)-D-glucopyranose**.

That is, two **D-glucopyranose** rings joined by an **α(1→4) glycosidic bond**:
- the **anomeric carbon of the left glucose** is involved in the glycosidic bond and is **α**
- the **right glucose** is the **reducing end**, so its anomeric carbon is free and may be α/β; the usual cyclic structure can be drawn with either anomer at the reducing end.

So the required cyclic structure is:
\[
\boxed{\alpha\text{-D-glucopyranosyl-(1→4)-D-glucopyranose}}
\]

---

# 4.2

## 4.2(a) Positive Tollen's test in test tube
After starch hydrolysis, reducing sugars such as **glucose** are formed. Glucose reduces Tollen’s reagent.

Balanced equation:
\[
\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6 + 2[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+ + 3OH^- \rightarrow C_6H_{11}O_7^- + 2Ag(s) + 4NH_3 + 2H_2O}
\]

Equivalent molecular form:
\[
\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6 + 2[Ag(NH_3)_2]OH \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_7 + 2Ag + 4NH_3 + H_2O}
\]

Reactant: open-chain **D-glucose**  
Product: **D-gluconic acid / gluconate**

---

## 4.2(b) Reactions in Step iv causing grey-black colour all over TLC plate
The plate was first dipped in \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\), then in \(\mathrm{NaOH}\). This gives silver oxide / silver hydroxide type dark deposit over the plate.

Main reaction:
\[
\mathrm{2AgNO_3 + 2NaOH \rightarrow Ag_2O(s) + 2NaNO_3 + H_2O}
\]

(\(\mathrm{AgOH}\) formed initially is unstable and converts to \(\mathrm{Ag_2O}\))

\[
\mathrm{2AgOH \rightarrow Ag_2O + H_2O}
\]

This causes the brownish-black background.

---

## 4.2(c) Reaction causing disappearance of black colour in Step v
Sodium thiosulfate dissolves silver oxide/silver salts by complex formation.

A suitable balanced reaction is:
\[
\mathrm{Ag_2O + 4S_2O_3^{2-} + H_2O \rightarrow 2[Ag(S_2O_3)_2]^{3-} + 2OH^-}
\]

This removes the black background from most of the plate.

---

## 4.2(d) Reaction responsible for coloured maltose spot
At the maltose spot, reducing sugar reduces silver(I) to silver metal, giving the dark spot.

Balanced equation for maltose:
\[
\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11} + 2[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+ + 3OH^- \rightarrow C_{12}H_{21}O_{12}^- + 2Ag(s) + 4NH_3 + 2H_2O}
\]

That is, **maltose** is oxidized to **maltobionate (or maltobionic acid in neutral form)**, while Ag(I) is reduced to Ag(0).

---

## 4.2(e) Identities of A, D, F
Given:
- B = oligosaccharides
- E = maltose

High \(R_f\) spots A and D are the smallest, most mobile carbohydrate → **glucose**.  
F lies below maltose and above oligosaccharides → **maltotriose**.

So:
- \(\boxed{A = \text{glucose}}\)
- \(\boxed{D = \text{glucose}}\)
- \(\boxed{F = \text{maltotriose}}\)

---

## 4.2(f) Correct options from TLC behavior
Silica gel is polar, so compounds with more OH groups interact more strongly and move less. Larger carbohydrates therefore have lower mobility.

Thus:
- (A) false
- (B) false
- (C) false
- (D) true

\[
\boxed{(D)}
\]

---

# 4.3

## 4.3(a) Structures of Y and Z
Phenol + conc. \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) with carbohydrates gives dehydration products from sugars.  
For hexoses, the intermediate is **5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF)**.

So:

### Intermediate Y, \( \mathrm{C_6H_6O_3} \)
\[
\boxed{\text{5-hydroxymethylfurfural}}
\]
Structure: furan ring with
- CHO at 2-position
- CH2OH at 5-position

### Product Z, \( \mathrm{C_{18}H_{14}O_4} \)
This is the condensation product of **HMF with two phenol molecules**.

\[
\boxed{\text{bis(phenyl)-substituted derivative formed from 1 HMF + 2 phenol}}
\]

More specifically, it is the phenol-condensation product of HMF:
**4,4'-dihydroxydiphenylmethyl-substituted furan aldehyde type product**, consistent with \( \mathrm{C_{18}H_{14}O_4} \).

---

## 4.3(b) Reaction causing decrease in intensity ratio \(I(D):I(E)\)
Student 3 used phenol-acid reagent, under which **maltose can hydrolyse to glucose** on the TLC plate.  
This decreases the maltose spot intensity E and increases glucose-derived colour, altering the ratio.

Balanced equation:
\[

\]

## 4.3(c) Comparison of \(I(F):I(B)\) between student 3 and student 2
Here:

Under phenol-acid, these species can also hydrolyse on the plate, but spotting volumes may differ. Therefore the ratio cannot be guaranteed to be always higher or always lower.

**Problem 5: A purple haze (19 Marks)**

Iodine is a purple-black crystalline solid at room temperature that has a unique ability to sublime into a violet-purple vapour.
Iodine was accidentally discovered by French chemist Bernard Courtois while preparing potassium nitrate for gunpowder. He took seaweed ash and mixed it with sulfuric acid. The mixture gave off purple vapour, which then formed shiny purplish-black crystals on the sides of the vessel. Courtois had discovered solid iodine!

**5.1.** The ground-state electronic configuration of iodine atom is represented by:
(a) $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^24p^5$
(b) $[\text{Xe}]5d^{10}6s^26p^5$
(c) $[\text{Kr}]4d^{10}5s^25p^5$
(d) $[\text{Ar}]4d^{10}5s^25p^5$

**Part A: Extraction of Iodine**
Iodine discovery had a profound impact on medical practice. Many commercial uses evolved, including as a disinfectant, in pharmaceuticals, as a catalyst, pigments for ink, etc. Radioactive isotopes of iodine are today used to treat thyroid cancer.
Elemental iodine is not naturally found in its free state. It is found in seaweeds as iodide ($\text{I}^-$), and in caliche (saltpetre deposits) and associated groundwaters as iodate ($\text{IO}_3^-$).

**5.2.** Write the balanced chemical equation(s) of the reaction(s) which produced iodine in the accidental discovery by Bernard Courtois.

To meet the growing market demand, extraction of iodine from natural resources has grown, with Chile and Japan as the leading producers. The commercial recovery of iodine depends on the source. Two of the methods are given below -

**Method 1 (From iodates):** To heaps of Chilean saltpetre containing trace amounts of iodates, water is poured to dissolve the saltpetre and the iodate. After crystalizing out nitrate salts, the mother liquor is collected, concentrated and divided into two parts.
i. One part of the concentrate is first reduced with slight excess of sodium bisulphite to give iodide.
ii. The solution obtained in step i is then mixed with the remaining concentrate to yield iodine.

**5.3.** Write balanced ionic equations for the two steps in the production of iodine from iodate.
**5.4.** Write the oxidation number of all iodine species in the above reaction mixture.
**5.5.** The nature of solution in step ii after iodine formation is:
(a) acidic
(b) basic
(c) neutral

**Method 2 (From iodide):** Iodide solution from natural sources is first treated with aqueous copper sulphate and ferrous sulphate. The white solid that precipitates out is filtered, washed with water, dried, and finely ground. This purified white solid is then heated with potassium carbonate solution to give potassium iodide solution and a red-brown precipitate. The precipitate is filtered off and the solution is oxidized with sodium dichromate and sulfuric acid to liberate iodine.

**5.6.** Write balanced chemical equations for the three steps described in Method 2.

Common table salt is "iodised" by the addition of potassium iodide or iodate. In an experiment, 50 g of iodised salt (containing iodate) was dissolved in 250 mL water. To 50 mL of this salt solution taken in a 250 mL conical flask, 2 mL of 2 M sulphuric acid and 5 mL of 0.6 M potassium iodide solution were added. The yellow-brown solution obtained was titrated against 0.002 M sodium thiosulfate until solution colour in the flask became very pale. Then 1 mL of starch indicator was added, and the titration was continued till the dark blue-black colour completely disappeared. The burette reading was 12.4 mL.

**5.7.** Write balanced chemical equations for the reactions involved in titration and calculate the iodine content (in mg) per kg of salt.

**Part-II: Bonding and Colour of Iodine**
Iodine exists as a highly coloured diatomic molecule and the colour arises from an electronic transition between the molecular orbitals (MOs) of iodine.

**5.8.** Assign labels to appropriate MO shape of $\text{I}_2$ molecules arising from the valence shell atomic orbitals (AOs) of two iodine atoms. Take z-axis as the internuclear axis. Four of the eight labels are given: $\sigma_{5s}$, $\sigma^*_{5s}$, $\pi_{5p_x}$, $\pi_{5p_y}$.
The shapes to label are described below:
- Shape 1: Two p-orbitals oriented along the internuclear (z) axis, overlapping out-of-phase (with a nodal plane between the nuclei).
- Shape 2: Two p-orbitals oriented perpendicular to the internuclear axis, overlapping in-phase side-on.
- Shape 3: Two p-orbitals oriented perpendicular to the internuclear axis (orthogonal to Shape 2), overlapping in-phase side-on.
- Shape 4: Two p-orbitals oriented perpendicular to the internuclear axis, overlapping out-of-phase side-on (with a nodal plane between the nuclei).
- Shape 5: Two s-orbitals overlapping out-of-phase (with a nodal plane between the nuclei).
- Shape 6: Two p-orbitals oriented along the internuclear (z) axis, overlapping in-phase head-on.
- Shape 7: Two s-orbitals overlapping in-phase.
- Shape 8: Two p-orbitals oriented perpendicular to the internuclear axis (orthogonal to Shape 4), overlapping out-of-phase side-on.

**5.9.** A blank MO energy level diagram is provided for the valence shell of $\text{I}_2$. The diagram shows the 5s atomic orbitals combining to form a lower and an upper MO, and the 5p atomic orbitals combining to form a lowest MO, two degenerate MOs above it, two degenerate MOs above that, and one highest MO. Label the MOs and state the electron configuration of the $\text{I}_2$ molecule by listing the filled MOs in order of increasing energy, along with the number of electrons in each.

**5.10.** The violet colour of iodine vapour is a result of the excitation of electron(s) between molecular orbitals. Identify the MOs involved in this electronic transition in initial and final state.

**5.11.** Iodine has poor solubility in water, but solubility increases in KI solution due to formation of the triiodide ion $\text{I}_3^-$. Identify the AO of $\text{I}^-$ and MO of $\text{I}_2$ which combine to form the HOMO in triiodide ion.

## 5.1
Iodine, \(Z=53\), has ground-state configuration:

\[
\boxed{[\mathrm{Kr}]\,4d^{10}5s^25p^5}
\]

So the correct option is:

\[
\boxed{(c)}
\]

---

# 5.2
Seaweed ash contains iodides. On treatment with sulfuric acid, first HI is formed, and then HI is oxidized by concentrated sulfuric acid to iodine.

Balanced equations:

\[
\mathrm{KI + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow KHSO_4 + HI}
\]

and

\[
\mathrm{2HI + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow I_2 + SO_2 + 2H_2O}
\]

(If the iodide salt is NaI, analogous equation applies.)

---

# 5.3
Method 1: from iodate

## Step i: reduction of iodate to iodide by bisulfite
Balanced ionic equation:

\[
\mathrm{IO_3^- + 3HSO_3^- \rightarrow I^- + 3HSO_4^-}
\]

## Step ii: iodate reacts with iodide to give iodine
Balanced ionic equation:

\[
\mathrm{IO_3^- + 5I^- + 6H^+ \rightarrow 3I_2 + 3H_2O}
\]

---

# 5.4
Oxidation numbers of iodine species:

- in \(\mathrm{IO_3^-}\): \(\boxed{+5}\)
- in \(\mathrm{I^-}\): \(\boxed{-1}\)
- in \(\mathrm{I_2}\): \(\boxed{0}\)

---

# 5.5
In step ii, reaction is

\[
\mathrm{IO_3^- + 5I^- + 6H^+ \rightarrow 3I_2 + 3H_2O}
\]

Since \(H^+\) is required, the solution is **acidic**.

\[
\boxed{(a)\ \text{acidic}}
\]

---

# 5.6
Method 2: from iodide

## Step 1: precipitation with copper sulfate and ferrous sulfate
Ferrous ion reduces \(Cu^{2+}\) to \(Cu^+\), which precipitates iodide as CuI.

\[
\mathrm{2CuSO_4 + 4KI + 2FeSO_4 \rightarrow 2CuI(s) + I_2 + Fe_2(SO_4)_3 + 2K_2SO_4}
\]

The iodine formed is then reduced by excess \(Fe^{2+}\), so net precipitation step can be written as:

\[
\boxed{\mathrm{2Cu^{2+} + 4I^- + 2Fe^{2+} \rightarrow 2CuI(s) + 2Fe^{3+} + 2I^-}}
\]

which simplifies to:

\[
\boxed{\mathrm{2Cu^{2+} + 2I^- + 2Fe^{2+} \rightarrow 2CuI(s) + 2Fe^{3+}}}
\]

## Step 2: heating CuI with potassium carbonate
This gives KI solution and cuprous oxide (red-brown precipitate):

\[
\boxed{\mathrm{2CuI + K_2CO_3 \rightarrow 2KI + Cu_2O(s) + CO_2}}
\]

## Step 3: oxidation of iodide with dichromate in acid
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 14H^+ + 6I^- \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+} + 3I_2 + 7H_2O}}
\]

Equivalent molecular form with sodium dichromate and sulfuric acid is also acceptable.

---

# 5.7
## Reactions involved in titration

### Liberation of iodine from iodate by iodide in acid
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{IO_3^- + 5I^- + 6H^+ \rightarrow 3I_2 + 3H_2O}}
\]

### Titration of iodine with thiosulfate
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{I_2 + 2S_2O_3^{2-} \rightarrow 2I^- + S_4O_6^{2-}}}
\]

---

## Calculation of iodine content

Thiosulfate used:

\[
C = 0.002\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}},\quad V = 12.4\ \mathrm{mL}=0.0124\ \mathrm{L}
\]

\[
n(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}})=0.002\times0.0124=2.48\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol}
\]

From
\[
\mathrm{I_2 + 2S_2O_3^{2-} \rightarrow 2I^- + S_4O_6^{2-}}
\]

\[
n(I_2)=\frac{2.48\times10^{-5}}{2}=1.24\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol}
\]

From
\[
\mathrm{IO_3^- + 5I^- + 6H^+ \rightarrow 3I_2 + 3H_2O}
\]

\[
n(IO_3^-)=\frac{1.24\times10^{-5}}{3}=4.133\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{mol}
\]

This is in **50 mL** aliquot.  
Total solution volume = 250 mL, so total moles in 50 g salt sample:

\[
n_{\text{total}}=5\times4.133\times10^{-6}=2.067\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol}
\]

Mass of iodine in iodate per 50 g salt:
Each mole of iodate contains 1 mole of iodine atoms.

\[
m(I)=2.067\times10^{-5}\times126.9\approx2.62\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{g}
\]

\[
=2.62\ \mathrm{mg}
\]

This is in **50 g** salt, so per kg:

\[
2.62\times\frac{1000}{50}=52.4\ \mathrm{mg\,kg^{-1}}
\]

\[
\boxed{52.4\ \mathrm{mg\ of\ iodine\ per\ kg\ of\ salt}}
\]

---

# 5.8
Label the MO shapes.

Given z-axis is internuclear axis.

- Shape 1: out-of-phase head-on \(p_z\) overlap  
  \[
  \boxed{\sigma^*_{5p_z}}
  \]

- Shape 2: in-phase side-on \(p\) overlap  
  \[
  \boxed{\pi_{5p_x}}
  \]

- Shape 3: in-phase side-on, orthogonal to shape 2  
  \[
  \boxed{\pi_{5p_y}}
  \]

- Shape 4: out-of-phase side-on  
  \[
  \boxed{\pi^*_{5p_x}}
  \]

- Shape 5: out-of-phase \(s-s\) overlap  
  \[
  \boxed{\sigma^*_{5s}}
  \]

- Shape 6: in-phase head-on \(p_z\) overlap  
  \[
  \boxed{\sigma_{5p_z}}
  \]

- Shape 7: in-phase \(s-s\) overlap  
  \[
  \boxed{\sigma_{5s}}
  \]

- Shape 8: out-of-phase side-on, orthogonal to shape 4  
  \[
  \boxed{\pi^*_{5p_y}}
  \]

---

# 5.9
Each I atom contributes 7 valence electrons, so \(\mathrm{I_2}\) has 14 valence electrons.

For halogen diatomics, valence MO order is:

\[
\sigma_{5s} < \sigma^*_{5s} < \sigma_{5p_z} < \pi_{5p_x}=\pi_{5p_y} < \pi^*_{5p_x}=\pi^*_{5p_y} < \sigma^*_{5p_z}
\]

Now fill 14 electrons:

\[
\boxed{(\sigma_{5s})^2(\sigma^*_{5s})^2(\sigma_{5p_z})^2(\pi_{5p_x})^2(\pi_{5p_y})^2(\pi^*_{5p_x})^2(\pi^*_{5p_y})^2}
\]

Highest occupied MO (HOMO): \(\pi^*_{5p}\)  
Lowest unoccupied MO (LUMO): \(\sigma^*_{5p_z}\)

---

# 5.10
The visible violet colour comes from excitation of an electron from HOMO to LUMO:

\[
\boxed{\pi^*_{5p} \rightarrow \sigma^*_{5p_z}}
\]

More explicitly:

\[
\boxed{\pi^*_{5p_x}\ \text{or}\ \pi^*_{5p_y}\ \rightarrow\ \sigma^*_{5p_z}}
\]

---

# 5.11
In \(\mathrm{I_3^-}\), the HOMO forms by interaction of:
- the filled **5p orbital of \(I^-\)** aligned along the molecular axis
- the **\(\sigma^*_{5p_z}\)** MO of \(\mathrm{I_2}\)

So:

\[
\boxed{\text{AO of } I^-: 5p_z}
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{MO of } I_2: \sigma^*_{5p_z}}
\]

---
